frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control through Sonatrach, but European demand, pricing, and infrastructure partnerships constrain strategic flexibility. Hydrocarbon dependence remains a structural vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Southern Border Instability
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's non-interventionist regional posture. External military and energy competition adds pressure around the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Angola controls its hydrocarbons institutionally but remains highly dependent on foreign operators, external technology, and volatile oil revenues. Debt and financing relationships continue to narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Strategic Contest
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting competing U.S., European, Chinese, and Gulf interests because of its access to Central African copper and cobalt. Infrastructure investment could diversify Angola's leverage but also reproduce transit dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Transit Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain vulnerable to border closures, sanctions legacies, and disputes over oil-export and port access. Cotonou's regional importance gives Benin leverage but exposes it to retaliatory disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence from the Sahel is pressuring Benin's northern frontier and threatening roads, parks, and agricultural zones. Foreign security assistance is useful but increases reliance on external intelligence and equipment.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Market Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with De Beers and is pursuing greater domestic value capture, but diamond demand and marketing channels remain externally exposed. A prolonged market downturn would pressure public revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Water Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited water, power, and transport capacity restrict mineral-processing ambitions and raise dependence on regional corridors. New investment can improve resilience but may give foreign financiers influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgent Gold-Zone Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and informal networks continue to threaten gold-producing areas, transport routes, and state revenue collection. The government's push for tighter control is constrained by insecurity and limited administrative reach.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The break with several Western partners and deeper reliance on Russian security support have increased Burkina Faso's diplomatic autonomy from former patrons. They have also created new risks around opaque contracts, accountability, and external influence over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over gold and rare-mineral supply chains, but weak oversight, informal extraction, and reliance on foreign buyers limit value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Great Lakes security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and armed groups continue to constrain border security and national policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its ports, air links, and location between Europe, Africa, and the Americas, while remaining dependent on external capital and demand.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and external fisheries agreements generate revenue but raise concerns over enforcement, depleted stocks, and local control of marine resources.

highlights: Oil and gas remain externally financed

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon value capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and financing remain central to oil, gas, and major infrastructure projects, limiting domestic control despite state participation and localization efforts.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest regions disrupts roads, agricultural supply chains, and energy investment while increasing dependence on security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond concessions
frictionVectors.details: The state has limited capacity to regulate artisanal and industrial mining, leaving production vulnerable to opaque foreign intermediaries, armed groups, and off-budget arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-resources influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors remain influential in regime protection and mining networks, constraining Western leverage and complicating transparent resource governance.

highlights: Sahel security partnerships are being recalibrated

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector external control
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues dominate fiscal capacity, while foreign operators, lenders, and transit infrastructure retain substantial influence over production and export terms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign basing and security leverage
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown and repositioning of external military partners creates uncertainty around border security, counterinsurgency support, and the government's room for strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: French-Moroccan Influence
frictionVectors.details: France retains substantial leverage through Mayotte, migration management, aid, and maritime security ties. Moroccans and Gulf actors are also expanding diplomatic and commercial engagement, giving Moroni alternatives but limited bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Gaps
frictionVectors.details: Weak inter-island transport and limited port capacity constrain sovereign control over fisheries, trade, and offshore resources. External financing is essential for infrastructure, increasing exposure to politically conditioned investment.

frictionVectors.title: M23-Rwanda Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east continues to undermine state authority, displace communities, and affect mineral corridors. Kinshasa faces persistent allegations of external support networks and limited control over borderland trade.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in copper and cobalt production, processing, and infrastructure-linked contracts. Efforts to secure greater domestic value addition face governance, financing, and security constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain central to state finance, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price volatility and foreign operator influence. Limited diversification reduces the government's ability to convert resource rents into broad-based sovereign capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects strengthen connectivity but can increase dependence on external contractors and creditors. The Pointe-Noire corridor remains strategically important for export access and foreign commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Processing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has expanded domestic processing and producer-sector regulation, but global buyers and external financiers still capture substantial value. Climate stress and volatile prices could weaken gains in sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Gulf Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port expansion and transport links are attracting Gulf, Chinese, and European capital. Competition among partners improves financing options but may create long-term exposure through concessions, debt, and strategic logistics stakes.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and diplomatic weight but constrain independent security positioning. Rivalry among external powers makes Djibouti strategically valuable yet highly exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Port Concession Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, and logistics assets are central to the economy and closely linked to foreign capital and debt. The Doraleh dispute and China's infrastructure role illustrate the tension between immediate revenue and long-term control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: External financing needs, including Gulf investment and IMF support, constrain Cairo's room to manage ports, land, and infrastructure without foreign commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt exposed to perceived risks over downstream water flows and regional energy politics.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining or volatile oil and gas output keeps national revenue tied to foreign operators, offshore infrastructure, and opaque production-sharing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf and Asian project influence
frictionVectors.details: New port, logistics, and energy initiatives offer diversification but may deepen reliance on external contractors and capital rather than domestic value capture.

highlights: Mining remains a sovereignty fault line

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but create recurring concerns over concession terms, labor practices, and the state's effective control of mineral rents.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Gulf, Turkish, and other regional actors around Red Sea access increases the value of Eritrean ports while raising pressure on its strategic independence.

frictionVectors.title: Trade corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's access to ports, fuel, electricity, and major markets is heavily mediated through South Africa, limiting independent control over critical infrastructure and supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: External agribusiness leverage
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and textile exports remain vulnerable to foreign buyers, regional trade rules, and changing preference schemes, constraining domestic value retention.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD expands Ethiopia's control over electricity generation but continues to provoke acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and downstream assurances.

frictionVectors.title: External debt restructuring
frictionVectors.details: Debt negotiations and foreign-exchange shortages give creditors and international financial institutions leverage over economic policy, infrastructure priorities, and state-owned assets.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Mining renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese, iron ore, and timber while managing entrenched French, Chinese, and other commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon’s mineral exports depend heavily on foreign-financed rail and port infrastructure, limiting the state’s room to revise contracts without risking supply disruption.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty rests on regional backing
Fisheries and port access drive external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked security and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies on Senegal for regional security, transport connectivity, and market access, creating practical constraints on independent economic and foreign-policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and maritime control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited enforcement capacity threaten coastal resource sovereignty, while port modernization remains sensitive to outside financing and commercial influence.

highlights: Gold remains the central sovereignty asset

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage and illegal mining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and poorly regulated mining degrades land and water while allowing foreign-linked trading networks to capture value beyond effective state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is courting investment in lithium and other minerals, but fiscal pressures and infrastructure needs could produce contracts that prioritize rapid extraction over domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou infrastructure concessions
frictionVectors.details: The rail, port, and iron-ore complex gives foreign consortia major influence over Guinea’s export architecture, even as authorities seek higher state participation and local content.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite environmental and fiscal strain
frictionVectors.details: Rapid bauxite expansion has generated land, water, and community tensions, while opaque contracting and weak civilian accountability limit public control over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export earnings remain concentrated in raw cashew shipments, leaving producers and the state vulnerable to foreign buyers, price swings, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and trafficking exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and contested security structures make the port and maritime zone vulnerable to illicit networks, external political influence, and under-enforced commercial concessions.

highlights: Ports and energy remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and substantial Chinese infrastructure financing constrain Nairobi's room to set independent economic priorities. Debt-service pressure keeps transport and energy assets politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is seeking greater regional control over the Lamu port and transport corridor, while Gulf, Chinese, and neighboring-state interests compete for influence over logistics and energy routes.

highlights: Water exports deepen dependence on South Africa
Polihali project tests national bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Water sovereignty and treaty dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue but ties national resource security to South African demand, financing, and infrastructure access. Construction delays and cost pressures could weaken Maseru's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and mining vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned textile production and diamond mining provide employment and export earnings but leave the economy exposed to external market shifts and limited domestic value capture.

highlights: Port and corridor assets attract strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations generate fiscal revenue and jobs, but foreign concessionaires retain substantial control over production, logistics, and export chains. The government faces pressure to improve local processing and contract transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and major transport corridors depend heavily on foreign capital and operators, creating leverage for external partners over Liberia's trade and security priorities.

highlights: Oil revenue remains divided by rival authorities
Foreign security patrons shape infrastructure access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, terminals, and revenue flows. Production remains vulnerable to blockade threats and bargaining among domestic factions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, and other regional powers retain influence through security partnerships, bases, and energy interests. Their involvement limits unified Libyan control over strategic infrastructure and coastal corridors.

highlights: Critical minerals draw intense foreign interest
Weak state capacity limits local value capture

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects are important for export earnings but remain reliant on foreign capital, technology, and commodity markets. Fiscal and environmental disputes continue to challenge Madagascar's ability to secure a larger domestic share of value.

frictionVectors.title: Land, logging, and infrastructure pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed agribusiness, mining, and logging interests compete with local communities over land and transport access. Weak enforcement increases the risk that infrastructure expansion will deepen resource leakage rather than national resilience.

highlights: Debt restructuring opens room for resource-led growth

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mining Expansion
frictionVectors.details: The restart of Kayelekera uranium and proposed graphite and rare-earth projects rely heavily on foreign capital and operators. Malawi is seeking stronger state participation and local value addition while managing fiscal pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages, fuel-import exposure, and limited transport links constrain sovereign control over industrial development. Dependence on regional corridors through Mozambique remains a strategic vulnerability.

highlights: Junta asserts tighter control over gold production
Russian security ties deepen strategic dependence

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontations
frictionVectors.details: The government is renegotiating agreements with major foreign miners and seeking a larger share of gold revenues. Disputes over permits, taxes, and operating rights are increasing investor and diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-Resources Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support provides regime protection but narrows Mali's strategic autonomy. Persistent jihadist violence also threatens mining zones, transport routes, and state access to resource-producing regions.

highlights: Offshore gas enters a new phase of strategic importance
Iron exports remain central to economic sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and foreign operators offers major revenue potential but leaves Mauritania dependent on external technology, finance, and export infrastructure. Cross-border governance and revenue-sharing remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore Logistics Concentration
frictionVectors.details: SNIM remains a central national asset, yet rail and port capacity are concentrated along export corridors vulnerable to disruption. Chinese and other foreign investment is important for expansion but can limit domestic value capture.

highlights: Institutions preserve strong control over strategic assets
Indian Ocean sovereignty remains under negotiation

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Sovereignty Transition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is pursuing implementation of arrangements intended to resolve the Chagos sovereignty dispute while preserving a major foreign military facility on Diego Garcia. The process carries legal, diplomatic, and regional-security uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius must balance Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf commercial and security interests around Port Louis and its exclusive economic zone. External infrastructure and maritime partnerships create opportunity but raise concerns over strategic dependence.

highlights: State-backed industrial policy strengthens phosphate leverage
Renewables and Atlantic infrastructure expand strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and development of Western Sahara underpin phosphate, fisheries, and renewable-energy strategies but remain contested by Algeria and the Polisario Front. International legal and diplomatic disputes continue to affect foreign investment risk.

frictionVectors.title: Green-Industry External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is attracting European and Gulf capital for hydrogen, renewables, ports, and automotive supply chains. These partnerships support industrial upgrading but may leave technology, financing, and export access vulnerable to external conditions.

highlights: LNG Restart Hinges on Cabo Delgado Security
Maputo Seeks Greater Local Value Capture

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity continues to threaten gas infrastructure and constrain state authority in the north. Foreign military and security support remains central to protecting strategic energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies retain substantial influence over project financing, technology, and export arrangements. Maputo is pressing for domestic employment, revenues, and infrastructure benefits without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Oil Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have increased Namibia's leverage but also its dependence on foreign operators, capital, and technical expertise. The government is seeking stronger local-content and fiscal arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: European and Gulf-backed projects could accelerate industrial development while leaving Namibia reliant on external financing and export markets. Domestic power, water, and skills constraints limit near-term control over the value chain.

highlights: Junta Tightens Grip on Uranium and Oil

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and revised terms in strategic mining, challenging established European commercial influence. Weak logistics, sanctions exposure, and limited technical capacity constrain Niger's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces has increased reliance on Russian-linked security assistance and regional military coordination. Persistent jihadist violence limits effective state control over resource-producing and transport corridors.

highlights: Oil Reform Meets Persistent Production Losses
Gas and Refining Ambitions Gain Momentum

frictionVectors.title: Crude Theft and Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Theft, sabotage, and underinvestment continue to reduce public returns from hydrocarbons while increasing dependence on private security and international operators. Production recovery remains vulnerable to regional instability and infrastructure failures.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Refining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: New refining capacity could reduce import dependence, but financing, crude supply, and technology links remain internationally exposed. Fiscal pressure and opaque contracting continue to weaken the state's bargaining position over resource rents.

highlights: State Control of Strategic Minerals Tightens
Eastern Congo Keeps Regional Pressure High

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and mineral-trading networks face sustained international scrutiny over alleged links to armed groups in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Sanctions or traceability demands could affect export access and investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strong state coordination provides Kigali with substantial control over infrastructure and strategic sectors, but the economy remains reliant on external aid, concessional finance, and foreign investment. Shifts in donor policy could narrow Rwanda's room for maneuver.

highlights: Gulf of Guinea energy hopes remain unrealized
Maritime partnerships protect a vulnerable blue economy

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon prospects remain commercially unproven, leaving São Tomé and Príncipe dependent on external operators and technical partners. Weak bargaining leverage limits near-term sovereign control over potential offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND MARITIME SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited surveillance capacity create pressure on national waters. Cooperation with Portugal and other partners improves security but also reinforces operational dependence.

highlights: Oil and gas revenues meet fiscal pressure

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACT RESET
frictionVectors.details: The government is reviewing contracts and seeking greater domestic value from the Sangomar and GTA projects involving foreign operators. Renegotiation risks disputes with investors and could delay production expansion.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: High debt and financing needs constrain Dakar's ability to fund ports, transport, and energy infrastructure independently. Gulf, Chinese, European, and multilateral capital remain important sources of leverage.

highlights: Tourism and strategic finance expose external dependence

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES ACCESS AND MARITIME CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from tuna licensing but must balance foreign fleet access with conservation and domestic processing goals. Limited enforcement capacity makes satellite monitoring and external maritime partnerships essential.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN STRATEGIC COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Port, coast-guard, and maritime-security cooperation draws interest from India, China, France, and other partners. Victoria seeks strategic flexibility while avoiding excessive dependence on any single external power.

highlights: Infrastructure investment is tied to external capital

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mineral projects remain central to exports and fiscal expectations, but foreign operators retain substantial control over capital, logistics, and marketing. Commodity-price volatility and contract disputes can weaken domestic bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAILWAY FINANCING
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked rail and port infrastructure improves connectivity but is closely tied to project investors and foreign lenders. The government faces pressure to secure public benefits without discouraging further investment.

highlights: Offshore oil ambitions intensify federal tensions
Ports and security remain externally shaped

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL LICENSING DISPUTES
frictionVectors.details: Foreign energy companies and Turkish partners are expanding interest in Somalia's offshore blocks, while federal and member-state authorities contest licensing and revenue-sharing powers. Weak institutions and insecurity make equitable resource control difficult.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, BASES, AND SECURITY PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, China, and Western actors compete for influence through port access, military support, and infrastructure projects. Somalia gains security capacity but risks fragmented sovereignty and dependence on external guarantors.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing of platinum-group metals, manganese and other strategic minerals while remaining dependent on foreign investment, technology and export markets. Competition among Western, Chinese and Gulf-linked firms complicates efforts to secure local value addition.

frictionVectors.title: GRID AND LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, rail congestion and port inefficiency continue to weaken sovereign control over mineral exports and industrial policy. Private-sector participation is expanding, but fiscal constraints limit the state's ability to modernize infrastructure on its own.

highlights: Oil revenues remain the strategic lifeline

frictionVectors.title: OIL TRANSIT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil sector depends on export infrastructure running through Sudan, leaving revenues exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption and bargaining pressure from external operators. The lack of diversified export routes sharply limits Juba's autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE AND EXTERNAL RESOURCE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and armed-group competition continue to shape control of oil revenues, land and transport corridors. Foreign commercial and security actors can negotiate access through local power networks, weakening transparent national oversight.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and oil assets
Ports and corridors become strategic prizes

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trade remain central to financing rival military networks, with cross-border smuggling and foreign-linked trading channels reducing state control over strategic resources. Competing external patrons use commercial access and logistics support to shape battlefield leverage.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA ACCESS AND INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated transport corridors are critical for humanitarian supply, military logistics and export access. External powers are competing for influence around the Red Sea coast while the conflict leaves infrastructure vulnerable to disruption.

highlights: Resource nationalism shifts toward value addition
Ports and corridors anchor regional leverage

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT AND PROCESSING PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pushing for stronger state participation, local processing and tighter oversight of gold, nickel and strategic-mineral projects. Negotiations with multinational investors can generate fiscal and legal friction as Dar es Salaam balances sovereignty with capital requirements.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL GEOPOLITICS
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam and central-corridor infrastructure increases Tanzania's regional leverage but attracts competition from Gulf, Chinese, Western and neighboring-state interests. Debt, concession terms and cross-border security will determine how much strategic autonomy these projects deliver.

highlights: Lomé consolidates its regional gateway role

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND EXTERNAL FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains a major source of commercial and strategic leverage, but its expansion depends on foreign capital, shipping networks and concession arrangements. This creates exposure to outside influence over customs, logistics and regional trade flows.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability spreading south from the Sahel are increasing pressure on northern transport and border infrastructure. Togo's security partnerships and military procurement choices may narrow policy flexibility as it seeks to protect trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: European Leverage over Migration and Finance
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia's dependence on European budget support, trade, and migration cooperation gives external partners substantial influence over domestic policy. Delays or conditionality around financing remain a sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Infrastructure Weakness
frictionVectors.details: Energy-import dependence and underperforming phosphate infrastructure limit Tunisia's control over strategic export revenues. Production disruptions continue to erode fiscal resilience.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Climate Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and associated fields promise major state revenue but remain exposed to sanctions risk, financing constraints, and pressure from Western climate-focused institutions. Tanzania transit dependence also limits Uganda's strategic flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important to transport and energy development, while repayment obligations narrow fiscal room. Uganda is balancing this relationship against Western security and development partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic processing, taxation, and transparency in mining, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and export channels. Copper price volatility leaves public finances vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and constrained rail and road links weaken Zambia's ability to capture value from minerals. Emergency power imports and regional transit dependence add external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capture of Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese investors remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, giving Zimbabwe access to capital while limiting immediate domestic control over technology, processing, and market access. Export restrictions are being used to encourage local beneficiation but enforcement remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Sanctions Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, sanctions-related financial barriers, and limited access to international capital constrain the government's bargaining power. The state remains reliant on opaque bilateral and private financing arrangements.
